So the changes that we made to goods cost recovery from one April this
year,
they were the culmination of a great deal of work, spanned several years, and
included extensive industry consultation and engagement.
We really had three main objectives for this piece of work.
We wanted to move to full cost recovery.
So we wanted the system to no longer have any taxpayer
subsidies, with some parts of the
fees and levies were charged to taxpayers.
We wanted to improve fairness for both fee payers and taxpayers, and we wanted to
make sure that the goods management system that we operate
on behalf of New Zealand was financially sustainable.
We think the work, and it's an extensive piece of work, we think we've achieved
those objectives.
And it was a culmination of a significant amount of
policy work,
and operational engagement and
consultation, including many meetings with industry.
So
you've specifically asked about the
equitability principle
and whether that was considered in calculating the levy rates.
So in
setting the levy rates and in going forward for consultation, we applied
the Order Office's good practice guide for setting and administering
fees and levies for cost recovery.
That guide sets out a core principle which talks about fairness and
equity as those who benefit from a service we provide,
or whose activities create the need for the service to be provided, should
meet the cost of providing it. So for Customs, we
clear and screen all imports and exports.
That comes at a cost. We provide a system to enable that
to happen. We receive information from importers and
exporters. The system operation comes at a cost.
We select goods out for intervention, examination,
ask for further information. There's cost associated with that.
There's a cost in risk goods in terms of investigations,
where we look to... There's a cost associated with the
process we may go through of inquiry and gathering evidence and trying to
identify who's responsible for the illicit shipment.
There's cost in our service delivery of the organization and
advice and support that we provide to
importers, exporters, businesses, consumers, et cetera.
So those are basically the activities that
we're looking to charge.
Fairness and equitability for levy payers means that they should
bear the costs of the services they create the needs for.
What that means is that they shouldn't shift their costs onto others.
Mm-hmm.
One of the points that we had in the previous system, there was a considerable
amount of cross subsidies where particular
streams of trade were paying for
other services.
Mm-hmm.
So for example, and this is totally relevant to this inquiry,
importers were covering the costs of customs going to search a ship when
we think the vessel owner should actually cover that cost of
service. They shouldn't also have other people's costs shifted onto them.
That's the same principle.
And there shouldn't be subsidies for taxpayers in particular
streams of trade that
gave them a competitive advantage over other streams of trade.
So one of our
significant concerns with this review was that mail
and fast freight,
a
significant amount of their costs were covered by taxpayers.
Whereas a retailer importing in high-value commercial
goods
had to pay full cost recovery. So we were very concerned about that when we started
that review.
When we undertook consultation, there was broad acknowledgement that the charges
should accurately reflect the costs that we incur for the service.
And I think it's a point that fairness does not mean that everyone pays the
same.
It means that they pay the costs for the activities they give rise to.
So that's how we applied that particular principle.
Do you mind if I just ask you a question about that too?
Absolutely.

consignment-

We're talking about who causes you to have costs.
Yes.
Yeah.

who caused the costs.
At the time.
Yeah.

they're spread over classes of levy payers.

It's for
each shipment of that class.

fairer. So just to point out that the move to consignment-based charging for goods
worth $1,000 or less eliminated a situation where some
freight firms were paying much less than others to clear a consignment.
So,
to explain,
we receive a cargo report from freight companies.
It could have anything from two consignments on it to
We screen all 1,000 consignments,
and we screen the two consignments obviously.
Those importers who were clearing goods on 1,000 consignments were paying exactly
the same-
Yeah
... as someone who paid two. And we removed the tax-paid subsidies
for low-value goods carrying
as freight or mail.
It means that customs and MPI's costs to process imports
and exports are no longer unsubsidized or partially subsidized
or fully subsidized or have any cross subsidies depending on how they cross the
border.
I just want to point out that in setting the rates and the actual
charges for this review, we applied an activity-based costing
methodology that had been externally reviewed and deemed to be a
sound methodology for assessing the actual costs
of each activity we undertake, and
allocating those costs to a fee or levy rate.
So, in the example I will give,
low-value fast freight, there's a process for clearance of goods.
If an officer opens a package in that process, we
allocate the costs of that officer opening the package to that
activity. If the same officer the next day
goes and works in the airport and searches a bag,
then the cost of that activity is allocated to the border processing
levy for travelers,
and so on.
Okay.
So that's the process for that.
The complaint appears to argue that the levy differences for goods carried as fast
freight and mail are unfair and distort the market.
We just want to point out that the different
levies for fast freight and mail are different
because they are different services. They are different products.
They have different processes. They have different service standards, institutional
arrangements, and legal frameworks.
So the key difference is in detail.
Fast freight, for low-value commercial fast freight,
freight companies and carriers provide a cargo report to customs prior to
arrival, which we screen,
and MPI also screens. We select out items for intervention, and
we send electronic messages back to the freight company clearing the rest of
the consignment. So what that means is that service gives
those freight companies certainty, reliability, predictability, and
speed. And all of this generally, unless we get the report late, happens before
the goods land in New Zealand. We've been told for many, many
years by the freight companies that that is the service standard that they would
like to receive from us. And it gives them predictability that
the vast majority of items they import
can meet consumer and supplier expectations of delivery
times. Mail
is cleared by customs after arrival.
We don't receive the same amount of structured
data
We require, because we don't receive the same amount of structured data, we put
officers in the international mail center where they view packages,
letters, and cards. So we do not provide the same level of
service in terms of speed, reliability, and
predictability. So those are two quite distinct services.
Okay.
And that's why there's a differential between how we wanted
to charge mail and how we wanted to charge fast
freight. Following the Office of the Auditor guidelines that,
we should treat the two activities differently.

We think more customers will shift to a mail stream because it's cheaper.
So those are the three points that we wanted to make.
The issue from our point of view is fairly simple.
So the regime that they've come out with for low-value goods-
Is it for any item coming through us will be charged $2.21
for customs and MPI.

delivered by a Freightways company,
that'll cost $2.21.
If the exact same item from the exact same

mail stream,
it'll be charged at about 27 cents.
So 27 cents through mail, $2.21 through us,
and we would argue the services are actually very similar.
In fact,
if you line hauled that mail through to New Zealand,
on an aircraft, and most mail will arrive on an aircraft,
the delivery time for that item through mail will be very similar
to through courier. Maybe it's a day later, but it won't be much

And so what we think will happen is customs or customers will start to shift.
They'll see that that's cheaper. And it's an industry where it's really
finely balanced in terms of pricing, so customers shift for 10, 20
cents on the freight fee, let alone maybe a dollar,
on that customs charge.
So, that's the big issue we have. Completely happy to pay our way, no problem

paying to what we will pay, 1,200% increase.

field.
So just to reiterate on the commercial impact, this is
a very commoditized market, particularly in the Asian market.
It's very price sensitive because we're talking about really low-value goods.
So we can lose business for a mere 5 or 10 cents.
So when you're talking about a $2 difference, that's a huge
incentive for a customer to move channels, and that is
driven by a government levy, which by definition for us is market
distortion.
If we go back to the irony of all of this, I think as has been mentioned even by
customs themselves, the data is very important to them.
So getting sophisticated data helps them protect the border.
The earlier they get that data, the sooner they can evaluate the risk
of each of those parcels. We provide that data pretty much from the time
the freight is in the air, even before it lands.
So it doesn't seem right that we would be penalized
for doing the very thing that customs and MPI
is asking of the industry to do to protect the borders.
If we talk about the efficiency piece, everything we do from a

electronic, and it's very fast. It's online.
So we're struggling to understand why that has a
higher cost to serve than the manual process that was
described in the NZ Post facility.
When that discussion was had with customs, when I challenged that, the
explanation that was given to me was not about the difference in
service, it was because NZ Post is effectively subsidizing
customs and MPI by giving them free rent, free car
parks, free systems. So of course, there's a lower cost to serve.
But it doesn't make sense or seem fair that because one
government organization is subsidizing another one, that that should set the
market rate. Levies by definition are supposed to empower them to set
an equal or reasonably equal levy across the
items. So,
making sure that the item
irrespective of which channel it goes through is charged the
same.
Thank you so much. I'm sure there are questions.
